unit.title: Interpreting and Discussing Results
unit.blurb: Frequency diagrams, time series graphs, stem-and-leaf diagrams and pie charts, choosing a representation, and comparing data with averages and the range.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Draw and interpret frequency diagrams for grouped discrete and continuous data.

O2.t: Draw and interpret time series graphs and describe trends.

O3.t: Draw and interpret stem-and-leaf diagrams, and find the median, mode and range from them.

O4.t: Draw and interpret pie charts, calculating angles and frequencies.

O5.t: Choose a suitable graph or chart for a set of data and explain the choice.

O6.t: Use the mean, median, mode and range to compare sets of data and draw conclusions.

p: A class records how long each student slept last night, to the nearest minute. The times range from 5 h 40 min to 10 h 10 min.
A bar for every possible time would be useless. How could you show the pattern? Think about it before you read on.
Discrete data is counted (number of pets); continuous data is measured (time, mass).
Put data into **classes** with **equal class intervals**.
Discrete: 0–4, 5–9, 10–14 … (no gaps, no overlaps between whole numbers).
Continuous: use inequalities so every value fits exactly one class: **6 ≤ t < 7**, 7 ≤ t < 8 …
For discrete grouped data, draw a bar chart with **gaps** and a label for each group.
For continuous data, draw a **frequency diagram**: bars with **no gaps**, and a continuous scale on the horizontal axis.
Label both axes and give a title.

p: Mia's phone app records the battery level every hour from 8 am to 2 pm: 100%, 88%, 75%, 66%, 52%, 40%, 31%.
Is the battery running down steadily? When might it reach 0%? Think about it before you read on.
Plot points and join them with straight lines.
A **time series graph** plots a quantity at **regular time intervals** and joins the points with straight lines. Time goes on the horizontal axis.
It shows the **trend** – the general direction of change (up, down, steady, seasonal).
The battery falls by about 11–13% per hour: a **downward trend**.
Points between plotted times are **estimates** (the lines are a guide). Continuing the trend predicts about 0% around 4–5 pm – but predictions far ahead are less reliable.

Step 4: Describe the trend; use the graph for estimates with care.

p: Fifteen students test their reaction times (hundredths of a second): 24, 31, 19, 27, 35, 22, 28, 41, 26, 33, 29, 18, 37, 25, 30.
How could you show all the values in order and still see the shape? Think about it before you read on.
Median = middle value in order; range = largest − smallest.
Split each number into a **stem** (tens) and a **leaf** (units). Write leaves **in order**, lined up, and give a **key**.
It keeps every value AND shows the shape like a bar chart on its side.
15 values → median is the 8th: **28**. Mode: none here. Range: 41 − 18 = **23**.

lesson.t: How do I draw and use a stem-and-leaf diagram?
p: Step 1: Choose stems (often tens) and write them in a column.

Step 3: Line the leaves up and add a key.
Step 4: Read off median (count), mode, range.

p: Two clubs show how their members travel there. In both pie charts the 'cycle' sector is **90°**. Club A has 40 members; Club B has 200.
Do the same number of people cycle to each club? Think about it before you read on.
Angle = fraction × 360°.

qq.prompt: What fraction of a pie chart is 90°?

p: A pie chart shows **proportions** (fractions of the whole), not actual numbers.
Both clubs: 90° = **¼** of members cycle. Club A: ¼ × 40 = **10**; Club B: ¼ × 200 = **50**.
So equal sectors can mean very different numbers when the totals differ.
To compare **proportions**, compare the angles directly.
To compare **numbers**, work out each amount: number = angle ÷ 360 × total.

lesson.t: How do I compare pie charts?
p: Step 1: Decide: proportion or actual number?
Step 2: For proportions, compare angles (or fractions).
Step 3: For numbers, use angle ÷ 360 × total for each chart.
Step 4: Explain your conclusion using both.

captions: A sports club has four sets of data: members' favourite sports, monthly attendance for a year, the times of a 400 metre race, and boys and girls in each age group.
Which kind of chart suits each one?
Start with the monthly attendance.
Which chart is best for attendance each month?
Pause the video and choose.
A time series graph, because the attendance is measured every month, and we want to see how it changes over time.
Remember the charts you know: bar charts, pie charts, line graphs, frequency diagrams, stem-and-leaf diagrams, and scatter graphs.
Choose the chart for the question you want to answer.
Your turn.
Which diagram sorts shapes by has a right angle, and is a quadrilateral?
Pause the video and choose.
A Carroll diagram.
It sorts items into a grid by two features: yes or no for each.
To justify a choice means to give a reason.
For example: a time series graph, because the data is attendance measured each month, and I want to see the trend.
Here is the method.
Step 1: identify the type of data: categorical, discrete, continuous, over time, or in pairs.
Step 2: decide what you want to show: a comparison, a proportion, a trend, or a relationship.
Step 3: pick the chart that shows that most clearly.
Step 4: justify your choice with a reason.
Favourite sports, as fractions of all the members: a pie chart, because it shows proportions of a whole.
40 race times, measured to a tenth of a second: a frequency diagram, because the data is continuous, with many values.
Boys and girls in each age group: a dual bar chart, to compare the two groups side by side.
Your turn.
Which chart shows the relationship between revision time and test score?
Pause and choose.
A scatter graph, because there are two variables for each student, and we want to see if they are related.
Amy wants to show monthly attendance through the year.
Which line is wrong?
Line 1 is wrong.
A pie chart hides the order of the months.
A time series graph shows the trend.
Use a time series graph.
Data journalists choose charts every day.
The same numbers can tell a clear story in one chart, and be confusing in another.
Choosing the right chart is part of telling the truth with data.
One last question.
What does justify mean?
Pause the video and choose.
Justify means give a reason.
To remember: match the chart to the type of data, and to its purpose.
Proportion: pie chart.
Trend: time series.
Relationship: scatter graph.
Comparison: a bar or dual bar chart.
Grouped continuous data: a frequency diagram.
Always justify your choice.

p: A cricket coach must pick one bowler. Runs given away per over in recent games:
**Asha**: 4, 5, 4, 6, 5 **Ben**: 1, 9, 2, 8, 5. Who should the coach choose? Try it before you read on.
Mean = sum ÷ count; median = middle; mode = most common; range = max − min.
Compare **an average** (how big the values are) and **the range** (how spread out / consistent they are).
p2: Averages are almost the same, but Asha's range is much smaller: she is more **consistent**. A coach wanting reliability picks **Asha**; one wanting the chance of a very good over might gamble on Ben.

p: **Mean** uses every value but is pulled by extreme values (outliers).
**Median** is not affected by extremes – good for skewed data like incomes.
**Mode** suits categorical data or the most popular size.

lesson.t: How do I compare data sets with statistics?
p: Step 1: Work out a suitable average for each set.
Step 2: Work out the range for each set.
Step 3: Compare: higher/lower average; more/less consistent (range).
Step 4: Write a conclusion in context, using the numbers.

p: Range = spread; average = typical size.
Sports scouts, teachers and businesses compare averages and spreads before making decisions.
Compare an average AND the range.
Smaller range = more consistent.
Median resists outliers; mode for categories.
Conclude in context with numbers.

To compare two sets of data, compare an average, which shows how big the values are.

Step 1: work out a suitable average for each set.
Step 2: work out the range for each set.
Step 3: compare.
Which average is higher?

The median is 31, which is more typical.

Team B is less consistent.

News reports usually give the median house price, not the mean.
